Sever

SEV-ur — stress on first syllable, rhymes with 'never' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To sever something is to cut it completely apart or forcefully separate it into pieces.

The storm severed the phone lines to the island.

Worked Example

When the earthquake struck, it severed the bridge from both its supports, leaving the island completely isolated from the mainland.

Sever is more precise than 'cut' because it emphasizes a complete, forceful, total breaking apart—not just a simple cut but a separation that ends all connection. The bridge's complete disconnection is exactly what sever names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

break: To break something is to snap or smash it apart — force applied until an object gives way. To sever is narrower and more final: it cuts a thing completely apart, ending every connection it had. A broken chair is damaged but still one thing; a severed cable is two pieces.

divide: To divide something is to split it into separate parts, usually on purpose and in an orderly way — a class into groups, a pizza into slices. To sever is violent and total: not portioning something out, but cutting it apart so the pieces no longer connect at all.

disconnect: To disconnect things is to end the link between them, often neatly and temporarily — you disconnect a hose or a call, and the ends can be joined again. To sever that link is to cut it apart completely and forcefully, with no easy way to put it back.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

join: to bring pieces together as one

unite: to bind separate things firmly together

Where it sits · how completely things come apart — separate → cut → tear → sever

separate vs. sever: Separate is much gentler than sever — separating things just moves them apart, while to sever is to cut them apart completely and often violently.

cut vs. sever: Cut is weaker than sever; a cut may be small or partial, but to sever is to cut something all the way through so the pieces come fully apart.

tear vs. sever: Tear is forceful but still weaker than sever — tearing rips something roughly, while severing splits it completely and permanently apart.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sever (from Latin separāre)

Root — sever (from Latin separāre): to pull apart, separate (se- 'apart' + parāre 'to arrange') (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Sever came into English whole from Latin separāre, 'to pull apart' — built long ago from se- ('apart') plus parāre ('to arrange'). That ancient sense survives exactly: to sever something is to cut or pull it completely apart.

Use the root in a new word: severance

Use the root in a new word: severance: When the company closed, workers received severance pay — money given when their tie to the job was cut apart, just as sever means to cut something completely apart.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Sever is dramatic and violent—the cutting apart of things that were connected or whole. Use it when describing forceful, complete breaks (relationships, communications, physical infrastructure). For routine cutting of objects into pieces, the plain word 'cut' is simpler and more natural.
